subChunks.title: Psychology, Crime & the Legal System
subChunks.hookHtml: In 1989, a 17-year-old named Jeffrey Deskovic was convicted of the rape and murder of a classmate in New York State, largely on the basis of a false confession obtained after seven hours of interrogation and a polygraph test that supposedly 'showed he was lying'. He spent 16 years in prison before DNA evidence exonerated him. His case was not an anomaly: the Innocence Project, which uses post-conviction DNA testing to review wrongful convictions, has exonerated over 375 people in the US alone — approximately 30% of them convicted partly on the basis of false confessions, and over 70% involving mistaken eyewitness identification. These are not failures of bad luck or isolated incompetence. They are systematic failures produced by psychological processes that courts, police, and juries have historically failed to understand: the conditions under which memories are unreliable, confessions are coerced, and witnesses honestly — and confidently — report things that did not happen. Forensic psychology applies psychological knowledge and methods to legal processes, criminal behaviour, and the justice system. It encompasses: understanding why people commit crime; assessing risk of reoffending; evaluating competency and mental state in legal proceedings; improving the reliability of eyewitness testimony and interview techniques; treating offenders; and consulting with courts and legal professionals. It is one of the fastest-growing applied psychology specialisms, and its findings have genuinely changed legal practice — though the pace of change has often lagged behind the evidence.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Scope of Forensic Psychology

Forensic psychology is often conflated in public perception with criminal profiling — a limited and empirically contested application. The actual scope is broader:

Criminal investigation   — investigative interviewing, eyewitness
                          testimony research, offender profiling

Legal proceedings        — competency assessment (fitness to plead),
                          mental state assessment (criminal responsibility),
                          expert witness testimony

Risk assessment          — structured assessment of reoffending risk,
                          violence risk, sexual recidivism

Offender rehabilitation  — evidence-based treatment programmes in
                          custodial and community settings

Victim psychology        — psychological impact of crime, trauma
                          assessment, victim-witness support

Eyewitness Testimony: Reliability and Reform

Elizabeth Loftus's research (1970s onwards) is foundational to understanding why eyewitness testimony — despite its compelling status in courtrooms — is an unreliable evidence source. Her laboratory studies demonstrated:

Post-event information effect: Information presented after an event is encoded is integrated into memory and can alter or replace the original memory trace. In Loftus & Palmer's (1974) classic study, the wording of a question about a car accident ('smashed' vs. 'contacted') altered participants' estimates of vehicle speed and whether they 'remembered' broken glass that was not present. Witnesses are highly susceptible to suggestions embedded in police questions, media reports, and conversations with other witnesses.

Confidence-accuracy dissociation: Eyewitnesses who express high confidence in their identifications are not more accurate than less confident witnesses — yet confidence is the primary factor determining how much weight juries assign to eyewitness testimony. This is one of the most replicated and practically significant findings in memory research.

Factors affecting reliability: Weapon focus (attention is captured by a weapon, reducing encoding of perpetrator features), cross-race effect (reduced identification accuracy for out-group faces), stress and arousal (moderate stress enhances attention but high stress impairs encoding), and retention interval (memory decays and is increasingly susceptible to contamination over time).

Reform evidence: Double-blind lineup administration (the officer conducting the lineup does not know who the suspect is, preventing inadvertent cues), sequential presentation (identifying photos one at a time rather than comparing them), and pre-lineup instructions ('the perpetrator may or may not be present') all reduce false identifications without substantially reducing accurate ones. These reforms have been widely adopted in the US and are increasingly standard in UK police practice.

Investigative Interviewing and False Confessions

The Reid Technique — a confrontational interrogation method involving psychological manipulation, minimisation of consequences, and presumption of guilt — was for decades the dominant police interview approach in North America. It produces high rates of confessions but is associated with a significant false confession rate, particularly in vulnerable populations (intellectual disability, mental illness, young people). Three types of false confession are identified:

Voluntary false confession    — without interrogation pressure
                               (to protect another, seek notoriety)

Coerced-compliant            — suspect knows they are innocent but
                               confesses to escape interrogation or
                               secure a promised benefit

Coerced-internalised         — suspect comes to believe they committed
                               the crime during interrogation

The UK's Achieving Best Evidence (ABE) framework and the PEACE interview model (Preparation, Engage and explain, Account, Closure, Evaluate) are evidence-based alternatives: information-gathering rather than confession-focused, non-confrontational, and designed to elicit accurate accounts from both victims and suspects. PEACE has consistently produced more reliable information than confrontational approaches and is now standard UK police interview practice.

Risk Assessment in Forensic Contexts

Risk assessment — estimating the likelihood of future offending — is central to sentencing, parole, and treatment decisions. Three generations of risk assessment:

  • First generation: Unstructured clinical judgment. Poor reliability and validity; subject to well-documented biases. Clinician predictions are barely above chance for long-term violence risk.
  • Second generation: Actuarial tools — statistical models based on static risk factors (criminal history, age at first offence, sex, relationship stability). Examples: Static-99 (sexual recidivism), PCL-R (psychopathy as a risk marker). Better predictive validity than unstructured clinical judgment but unable to account for dynamic (changeable) factors or individual context.
  • Third generation (Structured Professional Judgment — SPJ): Tools such as the HCR-20 (Historical, Clinical, Risk Management) combine evidence-based risk factors with structured clinical judgment, incorporating dynamic factors and producing structured risk management recommendations rather than probability scores. SPJ tools are now the standard in high-stakes forensic assessment in the UK.

Offender Rehabilitation: What Works

The 'What Works' movement in forensic psychology (Andrews & Bonta, 1990s) identified three core principles for effective offender rehabilitation:

Risk principle: Match intensity of intervention to level of risk — high-risk offenders require intensive programmes; low-risk offenders do not benefit from (and may be harmed by) intensive intervention.

Need principle: Target criminogenic needs — dynamic risk factors directly related to reoffending (antisocial attitudes, substance misuse, poor self-regulation, antisocial peer associations). Non-criminogenic needs (self-esteem, housing quality) should not be the primary treatment focus.

Responsivity principle: Use cognitive-behavioural approaches (general responsivity) and match delivery to individual learning style, cognitive ability, and motivation (specific responsivity). CBT-based programmes (Thinking Skills Programme, Sex Offender Treatment Programme, CALM — Controlling Anger and Learning to Manage it) have the strongest evidence base for reducing reoffending.

Mental Disorder and Offending

The relationship between mental disorder and offending is frequently misrepresented in public discourse. The evidence: people with severe mental illness are substantially more likely to be victims of crime than perpetrators, and the population-level contribution of mental disorder to violent crime is modest (approximately 3–5%). However, specific comorbidities — particularly antisocial personality disorder, substance use disorders, and psychopathy — are strongly associated with violence and recidivism. The insanity defence (not guilty by reason of insanity) is used rarely and successfully even more rarely; most mentally disordered offenders are convicted and serve sentences, sometimes in psychiatric rather than prison settings. The Mental Health Act (2007) provides powers to divert, detain, and treat mentally disordered offenders in appropriate settings.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen shows a clip from a documentary about wrongful convictions. A man describes the moment the interrogation broke him — not because he was guilty, but because he couldn't take the pressure any longer. 'Tell us what happened and you can go home.' He told them. He didn't go home for 11 years.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The psychology of false confessions explains something that intuition gets completely wrong. We assume innocent people don't confess because they know they didn't do it. But an interrogation room, after six or eight hours, is not a situation where normal reasoning applies. People in extreme stress are not calculating long-term consequences — they are trying to reduce immediate distress. And an interrogator who tells you 'just tell us what happened and this ends' is offering precisely that: relief, now, in exchange for consequences that feel abstract and distant. Vulnerable people — young people, people with intellectual disabilities, people in mental health crisis — are dramatically overrepresented in false confession data.

storyBeats.speaker: The misinformation effect in an eyewitness case
storyBeats.text: In a 1997 study by Loftus, participants watched a film of a car theft and were then, in post-event questions, given a 'detail' that had not appeared in the film — that the car was blue, when it was actually green. A week later, approximately 30% of participants confidently 'remembered' the blue car. In court, a confident eyewitness account is given enormous weight by juries. Understanding that confidence and accuracy are dissociated — and that post-event information can be indistinguishable from original memory — is fundamental to evaluating eyewitness evidence. The UK courts have improved significantly in directing juries on eyewitness reliability limitations, but the cultural assumption that confident eyewitnesses are credible remains powerful.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The 'What Works' literature in offender rehabilitation is one of the more important contributions forensic psychology has made to policy. For decades, the dominant view in criminal justice was 'nothing works' — rehabilitation is naive, and prison is for punishment and public protection. Andrews and Bonta demonstrated that the question wasn't 'does rehabilitation work?' but 'what works, for whom, under what conditions?' When the Risk-Need-Responsivity model is properly applied — high intensity for high risk, CBT-based cognitive skills programmes, targeting criminogenic needs — reoffending rates fall meaningfully. That's not soft: that's reducing future victims.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A forensic psychologist is asked to complete a pre-sentence psychological assessment on David, a 34-year-old man convicted of assault occasioning actual bodily harm following an altercation outside a pub. This is his third conviction for violent offences. He has a history of alcohol misuse, was unemployed at the time of the offence, and has a childhood history of significant physical abuse. He attributes the offence entirely to 'a moment of madness' and shows little apparent remorse. Previous community sentences have not been completed.

  1. Identify two static and two dynamic risk factors present in David's case, and explain why the distinction between static and dynamic risk factors matters for risk assessment and intervention planning.
  2. Using the Risk-Need-Responsivity model, explain how a rehabilitation intervention for David should be designed to maximise effectiveness.
  3. David tells the assessor he 'doesn't need any programmes — I just need to stop drinking.' Critically evaluate this claim in light of what the evidence says about criminogenic needs and effective intervention.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Static risk factors (historical, unchangeable): (a) Criminal history — three prior convictions for violent offences is a strong static predictor of future violence (appears in actuarial tools like HCR-20 and PCL-R risk scoring). (b) Age at first violent conviction — the earlier the onset of violent behaviour, the more entrenched the trajectory and the higher the actuarial risk. The distinction between static and dynamic factors matters for risk assessment and intervention because: static factors contribute to actuarial risk scores and help establish baseline risk level, but they cannot be changed by intervention (David's prior convictions will always be on his record). Dynamic (changeable) factors are the targets of intervention — because modifying them can genuinely reduce risk. Risk assessment using only static factors provides a stable estimate but cannot capture whether David is becoming more or less dangerous — longitudinal risk management requires dynamic factor monitoring.

Dynamic risk factors (changeable): (a) Alcohol misuse — substance misuse, particularly alcohol, is one of the most robust dynamic predictors of violent reoffending; it reduces inhibitory control and is often directly temporally proximate to violent incidents (as in this case). This is a clear criminogenic need — directly linked to the offending behaviour — and a primary intervention target. (b) Unemployment — unemployment is associated with reduced structure, increased exposure to antisocial contexts, and financial stress, and is a dynamic criminogenic risk factor. Employment and associated prosocial routine/identity are protective against reoffending.

2. RNR-based intervention design: Risk principle — David is high risk (three violent convictions, multiple criminogenic needs, non-completion of previous orders). High-risk offenders require intensive intervention; a low-intensity community intervention is unlikely to be effective and evidence suggests low-risk offenders are potentially harmed by high-intensity programmes. Need principle — interventions should target criminogenic needs: specifically, alcohol misuse (substance use intervention, motivational work), antisocial attitudes ('moment of madness' attribution — minimisation and externalisation of responsibility suggest cognitive distortions about the acceptability of violence and absence of responsibility-taking), and possibly antisocial peer associations (if the assault context involved a peer group where violence was normalised). Non-criminogenic needs (e.g., housing, self-esteem) should be supported as responsivity issues but are not primary targets. Responsivity principle — CBT-based cognitive skills programmes (e.g., Thinking Skills Programme, CALM — Controlling Anger and Learning to Manage it) have the strongest evidence base for violent offenders. These should be delivered by trained facilitators, with attention to David's literacy level, motivational stage (currently appears minimising), and specific responsivity for alcohol — which may require motivational interviewing before he is ready to engage with skills-based intervention.

3. Evaluation of David's claim: David is partially correct — alcohol misuse is a significant criminogenic need and reducing alcohol use is a legitimate and important intervention target. However, the claim that 'I just need to stop drinking' reflects an incomplete account that serves a minimising function: it attributes all responsibility to a single controllable factor while avoiding engagement with cognitive patterns (minimisation, externalisation of blame — 'moment of madness'), anger regulation deficits, and possible prosocial values deficits that the RNR literature identifies as important targets. The research evidence (Andrews & Bonta, 2010) consistently shows that addressing a single criminogenic need produces smaller effect sizes than comprehensive programmes targeting multiple needs concurrently. Moreover, David's statement that he 'doesn't need any programmes' is itself a dynamic risk factor — pro-criminal attitudes and resistance to intervention are associated with higher recidivism. A skilled forensic psychologist would explore this statement not as a correct or incorrect claim but as a starting point for motivational engagement: validating that addressing alcohol is important while opening exploration of other factors.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A defence barrister argues that eyewitness testimony should be treated as highly reliable evidence by courts because 'ordinary people have good memories and know what they saw.' Drawing on the psychology of eyewitness testimony, critically evaluate this claim and explain what reforms to court practice would be justified by the evidence. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The barrister's claim significantly overstates the reliability of eyewitness testimony. Research by Elizabeth Loftus and colleagues, across hundreds of studies, consistently demonstrates that memory for witnessed events is reconstructive, not reproductive: memory is not a video recording but an active process vulnerable to distortion at encoding, storage, and retrieval. The post-event misinformation effect shows that information received after the event — from police questions, media coverage, or conversations with other witnesses — can alter or replace original memory traces, without the witness being aware of the contamination.

The confidence-accuracy dissociation is particularly important for legal practice: eyewitnesses who express high confidence are no more accurate than less confident witnesses, yet confidence is the primary factor jurors use to judge credibility. Factors further reducing eyewitness reliability include: weapon focus (attention captured by a weapon, degrading face encoding), cross-race effects, high arousal/stress at encoding, and prolonged retention intervals during which memory is exposed to contaminating information.

Justified reforms: (1) Double-blind lineup administration — officers administering lineups should not know who the suspect is, eliminating inadvertent confirmatory cues. (2) Sequential presentation — showing photos one at a time prevents the relative judgement strategy ('which one looks most like the perpetrator?') that produces false identifications. (3) Judicial directions — juries should receive expert psychological guidance on eyewitness reliability limitations before deliberating. (4) Video-recorded initial accounts — the first witness account (closest to the event and least contaminated) should be preserved and available to the court. These reforms have been adopted in progressive jurisdictions and reduce false identifications without compromising accurate ones.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why memory is not like a video camera — and why an eyewitness who is completely certain about what they saw might still be completely wrong.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Loftus's (1974) finding that information received after witnessing an event can be incorporated into memory, altering or replacing the original memory trace. The witness is typically unaware of this contamination and reports the misinformation with genuine confidence.

The UK's evidence-based police interview framework: Preparation, Engage and explain, Account, Closure, Evaluate. Information-gathering rather than confession-focused, designed to elicit accurate and complete accounts while respecting the rights of vulnerable witnesses and suspects.

A personality construct characterised by superficial charm, lack of empathy and remorse, callousness, impulsivity, and persistent antisocial behaviour. Measured by Hare's PCL-R (Psychopathy Checklist-Revised). Associated with higher reoffending rates and instrumental violence; not synonymous with mental illness.

Andrews and Bonta's framework for effective offender rehabilitation: match treatment intensity to risk level; target criminogenic needs (dynamic risk factors); use cognitive-behavioural approaches and match delivery to individual learning style. The most empirically supported framework for reducing reoffending.

questions.questionHtml: What is the 'confidence-accuracy dissociation' in eyewitness testimony research?
options: More confident witnesses are significantly more accurate in their identifications
Eyewitnesses who express high confidence in their identifications are no more accurate than less confident witnesses, despite jurors rating confident witnesses as more credible
Accuracy of eyewitness recall declines over time but confidence remains stable
Eyewitnesses become less confident as they are exposed to misinformation
questions.correctAnswer: Eyewitnesses who express high confidence in their identifications are no more accurate than less confident witnesses, despite jurors rating confident witnesses as more credible
questions.explanationHtml: One of the most important and counterintuitive findings in eyewitness testimony research is that confidence does not reliably predict accuracy. A witness who says 'I'm absolutely certain that's the man I saw' is statistically no more likely to be correct than one who expresses uncertainty. Yet studies consistently show that jurors treat witness confidence as the primary indicator of reliability — rating confident witnesses as significantly more credible. This dissociation between confidence and accuracy has contributed to many wrongful convictions, including numerous cases later overturned by DNA evidence in which confident eyewitness testimony was the primary evidence against the defendant.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Research evidence indicates that people with severe mental illness are substantially more likely to commit violent crime than the general population, making mental disorder a major contributor to overall violent crime rates.
questions.explanationHtml: False on both counts. While severe mental illness is associated with a modestly elevated individual risk of violence (particularly when combined with substance misuse), the population-level contribution of mental disorder to overall violent crime is modest — approximately 3–5%. The vast majority of violent crime is committed by people without diagnosable mental illness. More importantly, people with severe mental illness are substantially more likely to be victims of violent crime than perpetrators. The public perception that mental illness is a major driver of violent crime is a significant and harmful stigmatising myth. Specific comorbidities — antisocial personality disorder, psychopathy, substance use disorders — are associated with much higher violence risk than diagnoses like schizophrenia or depression.

questions.questionHtml: A prison psychologist is designing a rehabilitation programme for a group of offenders assessed as high-risk for violent reoffending, many of whom have alcohol misuse problems. Using the Risk-Need-Responsivity model, which programme design is most consistent with the evidence?
options: A low-intensity self-help reading programme addressing self-esteem and personal development

An intensive CBT-based cognitive skills programme targeting antisocial thinking patterns, combined with alcohol intervention, delivered by trained facilitators with attention to individual learning styles
Counselling focused on emotional support and therapeutic alliance, without a structured curriculum
An employment and housing programme, since practical problems are the main drivers of reoffending
questions.correctAnswer: An intensive CBT-based cognitive skills programme targeting antisocial thinking patterns, combined with alcohol intervention, delivered by trained facilitators with attention to individual learning styles
questions.explanationHtml: The RNR model provides three clear principles for this group: (1) Risk principle — high-risk offenders require intensive intervention; low-intensity programmes (self-help, occasional counselling) are insufficient and evidence suggests they may even be counterproductive for high-risk groups. (2) Need principle — the programme must target criminogenic needs directly linked to reoffending: antisocial thinking patterns (addressed by cognitive skills programmes) and alcohol misuse are both strong dynamic risk factors for violence. Non-criminogenic needs like self-esteem (option A) or housing (option D) may need addressing as support but should not be the primary intervention target. (3) Responsivity principle — CBT-based approaches have the strongest evidence base for violent offenders (general responsivity); programme delivery should accommodate individual learning styles and motivational levels (specific responsivity). Supportive counselling (option C) without a structured CBT curriculum does not have evidence for reducing violent reoffending in high-risk groups.
